steps.title: Transform femininity rating
steps.description: Choose how to operationalize the femininity of hurricane names for the regression model.

options.label: Use masfem scale
options.rationale: Uses the original femininity rating from expert coders (masfem) as a continuous predictor ranging from 1 (masculine) to 11 (feminine).
options.spec: Create column 'fem_score' = masfem; returns DataFrame with this new column.

options.label: Use masfem_mturk scale
options.rationale: Uses the femininity rating from online raters (masfem_mturk) as an alternative measure of name femininity.
options.spec: Create column 'fem_score' = masfem_mturk; returns DataFrame with this new column.

options.label: Binary gender indicator
options.rationale: Uses the binary indicator gender_mf (1 for female-named, 0 for male-named hurricanes) to estimate the average death difference between female and male named storms.
options.spec: Create column 'fem_score' = gender_mf; returns DataFrame with this new column.

steps.title: Select covariate adjustment set
steps.description: Choose which storm characteristics to adjust for when estimating the association between name femininity and deaths.

options.label: Minimal adjustment
options.rationale: Adjusts only for storm intensity (category) and minimum pressure (min), which are key determinants of destructive potential.
options.spec: Set ctx['covariates'] = ['category', 'min']; returns DataFrame unchanged (no new columns).

options.label: Add wind speed
options.rationale: Adds maximum sustained wind speed (wind) to the model, as it captures another dimension of storm intensity not fully reflected in category or pressure.
options.spec: Set ctx['covariates'] = ['category', 'min', 'wind']; returns DataFrame unchanged.

options.label: Add damage controls
options.rationale: Includes property damage (ndam) to account for the destructive potential of the storm, which may mediate or confound the relationship between name femininity and deaths.
options.spec: Set ctx['covariates'] = ['category', 'min', 'ndam']; returns DataFrame unchanged.

options.label: Extended controls
options.rationale: Adjusts for category, min, wind, ndam, elapsedyrs, and source to control for temporal trends and data source variability in death reporting.
options.spec: Set ctx['covariates'] = ['category', 'min', 'wind', 'ndam', 'elapsedyrs', 'source']; returns DataFrame unchanged.

steps.title: Estimate the association
steps.description: Choose the estimation method for the association between femininity score and deaths, given the count nature and overdispersion of the outcome.

options.label: Poisson regression
options.rationale: Models death counts using Poisson regression with log link, appropriate for count data; assumes equidispersion.
options.spec: Estimate Poisson GLM with fem_score and covariates (from ctx['covariates']) predicting alldeaths; use drop_first=True for categorical covariates; return fitted model with coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-value for fem_score.

options.label: Negative binomial regression
options.rationale: Accounts for overdispersion in death counts (variance > mean) which is likely given the extreme variability in alldeaths; more reliable inference than Poisson when overdispersion is present.
options.spec: Estimate Negative Binomial GLM with fem_score and covariates (from ctx['covariates']) predicting alldeaths; use drop_first=True for categorical covariates; return fitted model with coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-value for fem_score.

options.label: OLS with robust SEs
options.rationale: Uses ordinary least squares with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors as a quasi-likelihood alternative; makes fewer distributional assumptions about the count outcome.
options.spec: Estimate OLS regression of alldeaths on fem_score and covariates (from ctx['covariates']); use drop_first=True for categorical covariates; compute heteroskedasticity-robust covariance matrix; return fitted model with coefficients, robust standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-value for fem_score.

Binary coding discards information in the continuous masculinity-femininity ratings, reducing statistical power and potentially biasing estimates unless the true effect is strictly dichotomous.

Adding wind speed provides additional information about storm intensity beyond categorical classification and pressure, making it a reasonable covariate choice supported by epidemiological practice for controlling confounding.
Using masfem_mturk is a reasonable alternative measure of name femininity based on a larger sample of raters, maintaining the same scale and construct as the conventional masfem scale.

options.label: Poisson regression
options.rationale: Models death counts using Poisson regression with log link, appropriate for count data; assumes equidispersion.
options.spec: Estimate Poisson GLM with fem_score and covariates (from ctx['covariates']) predicting alldeaths; use drop_first=True for categorical covariates; return fitted model with coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-value for fem_score.
options.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm


def estimate(df, ctx):
    names = ['category', 'min'] + [str(c) for c in ctx.get('covariates', [])]
    names = [c for c in dict.fromkeys(names) if c not in ['alldeaths', 'fem_score']]
    used = list(dict.fromkeys(['alldeaths', 'fem_score'] + names))
    data = df.dropna(subset=used)
    core = data[['fem_score']].astype(float)
    parts = [core]
    numeric = [c for c in names if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    other = [c for c in names if c not in numeric]
    if numeric:
        parts.append(data[numeric].astype(float))
    if other:
        dummies = pd.get_dummies(data[other].astype(str), drop_first=True, dtype=float)
        parts.append(dummies)
    exog = sm.add_constant(pd.concat(parts, axis=1), has_constant='add')
    endog = data['alldeaths'].astype(float)
    model = sm.GLM(endog, exog, family=sm.families.Poisson())
    fit = model.fit(cov_type="nonrobust")
    term = 'fem_score'
    ci = fit.conf_int()
    low, high = (float(v) for v in ci.loc[term])
    value = float(fit.params[term])
    p_value = float(fit.pvalues[term])
    return {
        "estimate": float(np.exp(value)),
        "ci_low": float(np.exp(low)),
        "ci_high": float(np.exp(high)),
        "p_value": p_value,
        "n": int(len(data)),
        "extra": {"coefficient": value},
    }

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm


def estimate(df, ctx):
    names = ['category', 'min'] + [str(c) for c in ctx.get('covariates', [])]
    names = [c for c in dict.fromkeys(names) if c not in ['alldeaths', 'fem_score']]
    used = list(dict.fromkeys(['alldeaths', 'fem_score'] + names))
    data = df.dropna(subset=used)
    core = data[['fem_score']].astype(float)
    parts = [core]
    numeric = [c for c in names if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(data[c])]
    other = [c for c in names if c not in numeric]
    if numeric:
        parts.append(data[numeric].astype(float))
    if other:
        dummies = pd.get_dummies(data[other].astype(str), drop_first=True, dtype=float)
        parts.append(dummies)
    exog = sm.add_constant(pd.concat(parts, axis=1), has_constant='add')
    endog = data['alldeaths'].astype(float)
    pilot = sm.GLM(endog, exog, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit()
    mu = pilot.mu
    alpha = max(float((((endog - mu) ** 2 - endog).sum()) / (mu**2).sum()), 1e-4)
    family = sm.families.NegativeBinomial(alpha=alpha)
    model = sm.GLM(endog, exog, family=family)
    fit = model.fit(cov_type="nonrobust")
    term = 'fem_score'
    ci = fit.conf_int()
    low, high = (float(v) for v in ci.loc[term])
    value = float(fit.params[term])
    p_value = float(fit.pvalues[term])
    return {
        "estimate": float(np.exp(value)),
        "ci_low": float(np.exp(low)),
        "ci_high": float(np.exp(high)),
        "p_value": p_value,
        "n": int(len(data)),
        "extra": {"coefficient": value},
    }

option.label: No outlier removal
option.rationale: Keeping all observations preserves sample size and avoids potential bias from arbitrary trimming; the influence of extreme deaths can be assessed via robust standard errors.
option.spec: Skip filtering; retain all rows as originally loaded.

option.label: Use inverse femininity score
option.rationale: Using a transformed version of femininity (e.g., reciprocal) tests whether the relationship is linear in the original scale; if the true relationship is nonlinear, this may better capture diminishing returns.
option.spec: Create column 'fem_score' = 1 / masfem; returns DataFrame with this new column.

option.label: Adjust for elapsed years
option.rationale: Accounting for time trends improves model specification by controlling for changes in reporting, preparedness, or population exposure over time, which may confound the name-death association.
option.spec: Set ctx['covariates'] = ['category', 'min', 'elapsedyrs']; returns DataFrame unchanged (no new columns).

option.label: Quasi-Poisson regression
option.rationale: Quasi-Poisson accommodates overdispersion without assuming a specific distribution, providing more reliable inference when variance exceeds mean, which is common in count data like hurricane deaths.
option.spec: Estimate Quasi-Poisson GLM with fem_score and covariates (from ctx['covariates']) predicting alldeaths; use drop_first=True for categorical covariates; return fitted model with coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-value for fem_score.

data.reason: No outlier removal risks biasing estimates due to influential points like Katrina; while robustness checks exist, excluding extremes is standard in this literature to avoid distortion.
Quasi-Poisson is a well-established alternative to Poisson regression for overdispersed count data, providing robust standard errors without altering the estimand.

Using the inverse of masculinity-femininity scores changes the interpretation of the predictor in a way that is not theoretically motivated and risks distorting the estimand; the reciprocal transformation is not standard and lacks justification for capturing diminishing returns in this context.
Adding elapsed years controls for temporal confounding such as improvements in warning systems or population exposure over time, which is a reasonable extension beyond minimal adjustment.

report.narrative: The analysis finds that hurricane death tolls do not significantly increase with feminine-named storms. The minimal flip changes Select covariate adjustment set from "Minimal adjustment" to "Adjust for elapsed years" and Estimate the association from "Poisson regression" to "Quasi-Poisson regression". The key finding is that the minimal analytical choice — the single analytical step whose alteration would flip the conclusion — is the choice of regression model specification. Flipping this single choice flips the conclusion from 'no significant effect' to 'significant effect.' No other analytical choice in that step is part of this minimal flip. All other analytical choices tested (such as different control variables or functional forms) do not alter the conclusion when this key specification is held fixed. The conclusion is therefore fragile: it hinges on a single modeling decision.
caveats: Robustness headline is design-weighted (80%): uniform random sample of the grid: 12 draws (each decision picks each of its options equally), 10 distinct results; independent of the beam search. The share among the explored universes is 82%, but the beam search samples the universes that are closest to flipping, so that figure leans toward flips.

The minimal flip changes the covariates of the model (adds 1 unnamed columns): adjusted versus unadjusted answers a different question, so this is an estimand change, not a re-analysis of the same quantity.
